## Why GPAbin?

Multiple imputation replaces each missing value with several plausible values,
giving you $m$ completed data sets instead of one. Numerical summaries such as
means and regression coefficients are then combined with Rubin's rules. But what
do you do when the "summary" is a *picture*?

If you construct a biplot from each completed data set, you get $m$ slightly
different pictures. You cannot simply average their coordinates, because a
dimension reduction solution is only determined up to rotation and reflection:
the same configuration can come out flipped, spun or mirrored from one
imputation to the next. Averaging unaligned coordinates would blur the display
into nonsense.

`GPAbin` solves this in three steps (Nienkemper-Swanepoel, le Roux and
Gardner-Lubbe, 2023):

1. construct a biplot for every imputed data set;
2. use **g**eneralised orthogonal **P**rocrustes **a**nalysis (GPA) to translate, rotate, reflect and scale
   all configurations onto a common target;
3. average the aligned coordinates, mimicking the pooling step of
   Ru**bin**'s rules, and draw a single unified **GPAbin biplot**.
   
The current version works with **categorical data**, using multiple
correspondence analysis (MCA) as the dimension reduction technique. In the
resulting biplot, points represent samples / observations and *category level points*
(CLPs) represent the response categories of each variable.

## Installation

### CRAN

```{r install-cran, eval = FALSE}
install.packages("GPAbin")
```

### Development version

```{r install-git, eval = FALSE}
devtools::install_github("jnienk/GPAbin")
```


## The workflow at a glance

Every step takes a `missmi` object and returns it with new elements added, so
the whole analysis can be written as one native pipe (`|>`):

```{r workflow-overview, eval = FALSE}
missbp <- missmi(implist) |>
  DRT() |>
  GPAbin() |>
  evaluation(compdat = compdat) |>
  plot()
```

| Step | Function | What it does |
|------|----------|--------------|
| 1 | `missmi()` | Prepares the input (a data frame with missing values, or a list of imputed data sets) |
| 2 | `impute()` | *Optional.* Multiply imputes a data frame with missing values |
| 3 | `DRT()` | Dimension reduction (MCA) on each imputed data set |
| 4 | `GPAbin()` | Aligns the configurations with GPA and combines them |
| 5 | `evaluation()` | *Optional.* Compares against a complete data solution, when one exists |
| 6 | `plot()` | Draws the biplot (`ggplot2` or base graphics) |

## The data: attitudes towards science

We use a real survey data set that is included in the `ca` package: `wg93`, the
West German sample of the 1993 *International Social Survey Programme* (ISSP) on
the environment. It contains 871 respondents. Four questions (`A` to `D`)
measure attitudes towards science on a five-point scale (1 = agree strongly to
5 = disagree strongly) and three demographic variables record sex, age group
and education. We keep the four attitude items together with age group (six
levels), giving five categorical variables.

```{r data}
data("wg93", package = "ca")
compdat <- wg93[, c("A", "B", "C", "D", "age")]
str(compdat)
```

Take note: All variables must be **factors**; `wg9`

### Creating missing values

This data set is complete, which is useful: we can delete some values on
purpose and then check how well `GPAbin` recovers the original picture. In reality, you would of course skip this step and start the pipeline with your incomplete data set.

We generate values that are *missing at random* (MAR): the chance that a person
skips questions `A` to `D` depends only on their age group, which is fully
observed, and increases with the age-group code (from 10% to 50%).

```{r missing}
set.seed(2024)
p_miss <- c(0.10, 0.15, 0.20, 0.30, 0.40, 0.50)[as.integer(compdat$age)]

missdat <- compdat
for (v in c("A", "B", "C", "D")) {
  missdat[runif(nrow(missdat)) < p_miss, v] <- NA
}

round(colMeans(is.na(missdat)) * 100, 1)  
```

About a quarter of the answers to each attitude question are now missing.


## Step 1: `missmi()`

`missmi()` is the entry point. It checks the data, records key dimensions and
the percentage of missing values and creates an object of class `missmi`. 
The printed summary reports: the number of imputations (`m`), the number of samples (`n`), the
number of variables (`p`) and the percentage of missing values (`miss_pct`).

It accepts either a data frame containing missing values or a list of already imputed data sets.

```{r missmi}
missbp <- missmi(missdat)
missbp
round(missbp$miss_pct, 1)
```

If your data contain no missing values, `missmi()` stops with a message,
because there is nothing to impute.

## Step 2: `impute()`

`impute()` creates $m$ imputed data sets with one of four available methods:

| `imp.method` | Approach                                         | Underlying function  |
|:-------------|:-------------------------------------------------|:---------------------|
| `"MIMCA"`    | Multiple imputation with MCA (the default)       | `missMDA::MIMCA()`   |
| `"jomo"`     | Joint modelling for categorical data             | `jomo::jomo1cat()`   |
| `"miceB"`    | Bayesian chained equations                       | `mi::mi()`           |
| `"mice"`     | Chained equations with polytomous regression     | `mice::mice()`       |

We use `"miceB"` with $m = 5$ imputations. Setting a seed makes the result
reproducible.

```{r impute, results = "hide", message = FALSE}
set.seed(927)
missbp <- impute(missbp, imp.method = "miceB", m = 5)
```

The imputed data sets are stored in `missbp$dataimp`, a list with one data frame
per imputation. They are complete:

```{r impute-check}
missbp$m
anyNA(missbp$dataimp[[1]])
```

## Step 3: `DRT()`

`DRT()` (dimension reduction technique) runs an MCA on each of the five imputed
data sets. For each imputation it stores the sample coordinates (`Z`), the
category level point coordinates (`CLP`) and the level names (`lvls`).

```{r drt}
missbp <- DRT(missbp)

length(missbp$Z)            
dim(missbp$Z[[1]])          
head(missbp$lvls[[1]], 6)   
```

Each of these five solutions is a perfectly valid MCA, but they are not yet
comparable: nothing forces the five configurations to share the same
orientation. That is what the next step takes care of.

## Step 4: Align and combine with `GPAbin()`

This is the core of the package. `GPAbin()` aligns the *m* configurations with
generalised orthogonal Procrustes analysis and then averages the aligned
coordinates.

```{r gpabin}
missbp <- missbp |> GPAbin()
```

Four new elements are added to the object:

| Element        | Contents                                                     |
|:---------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------|
| `Z.GPA.list`   | Aligned sample coordinates, one matrix per imputation        |
| `CLP.GPA.list` | Aligned category level points, one matrix per imputation     |
| `Z.GPAbin`     | **Average** sample coordinates, used for the GPAbin biplot   |
| `CLP.GPAbin`   | **Average** category level points, used for the GPAbin biplot |

To see what GPA did, we plot the category level points of all five imputations
(first two dimensions, one colour per imputation) before and after alignment.

```{r before-after-plot, fig.height = 4.5}
stack_clps <- function(clp_list, stage) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(clp_list), function(i) {
    data.frame(Dim1 = clp_list[[i]][, 1],
               Dim2 = clp_list[[i]][, 2],
               level = missbp$lvls[[i]],
               imputation = factor(i),
               stage = stage)
  }))
}

clps <- rbind(
  stack_clps(missbp$CLP,          "Before GPA"),
  stack_clps(missbp$CLP.GPA.list, "After GPA")
)
clps$stage <- factor(clps$stage, levels = c("Before GPA", "After GPA"))

ggplot2::ggplot(clps, aes(Dim1, Dim2, colour = imputation)) +
  geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ stage) +
  coord_fixed() +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  labs(colour = "Imputation") +
  theme_void()
```

On the left, the five MCA solutions are scattered: every imputation produced a
differently rotated or reflected picture, so a simple average would be
meaningless. On the right, after GPA, each category level is represented by a
tight cluster of five points. Averaging within each cluster gives the
coordinates in `CLP.GPAbin`.

By default the centroid configuration is used as the target. You can supply
your own through the `G.target` argument if you want to align to a particular
reference configuration.

## Step 5: `plot()`

`plot()` draws the GPAbin biplot. By default it uses `ggplot2`; use
`engine = "base"` for base graphics.

```{r plot, fig.height = 6.5}
missbp <- plot(missbp, title = "GPAbin biplot")
```

Dark points are respondents; gold squares are the category level points,
labelled `variable:level`. A respondent tends to have answered a question with
the category whose point lies nearest to them. The overall shape is the arch
that is typical of MCA on ordered response scales: for questions `A`, `B` and
`C` the extreme categories 1 and 5 lie at opposite ends of the arch and the
neutral category 3 sits at its apex. The age groups are all found near the
centre of the display, so age is only weakly related to the attitude
responses. Take note: the orientation of a biplot is arbitrary: a mirrored or rotated
version carries exactly the same information.

`plot()` returns the `missmi` object with the plot stored in `missbp$plot`, so
you can add to it like any other `ggplot` object:

```{r plot-custom, eval = FALSE}
missbp$plot + labs(subtitle = "Five imputations, aligned with GPA")
```

### Base graphics

```{r biplfig, fig.show = "hold", out.width = "75%"}
missbp |> plot(engine = "base", title = "GPAbin biplot")
```

### ggplot2

```{r ggbiplfig}
missbp <- missbp |> plot() |> evaluation(compdat = compdat)
```


Because these are ordinary `ggplot` objects, you can customise them further
with the usual `ggplot2` layers and themes.

## Step 6 (optional): evaluating against the complete data

Because we created the missing values ourselves, we know what the biplot of the
*complete* data looks like. `evaluation()` performs an MCA on the complete data supplied through `compdat`, and compares it with the GPAbin biplot. This is only possible for simulation studies or
examples like this one.

```{r eval}
missbp <- evalMeas(missbp, compdat = compdat)
missbp$tab
```

The table contains five measures:

* **1-PS**: one minus the Procrustes statistic. It measures how closely the two
  configurations match after the best possible rotation. Values close to 1 are
  good.
* **SP** (similarity proportion): the proportion of all responses for which the
  category predicted from the GPAbin biplot equals the category in the complete
  data. Observed responses are kept as they are, so they count as correct by
  construction (here `r round(100 * (1 - mean(is.na(missdat))))`% of all
  cells). Only the missing cells are actually predicted. Again, values close to 1 are good.
* **RPR** (response profile recovery): the proportion of respondents whose
  *entire* response profile is recovered correctly. This is a much stricter
  criterion than SP, with values close to 1 again reflecting successful recovery.
* **AMB** and **RMSB**: the absolute mean bias and root mean squared bias
  between the two configurations. Smaller values are better. They are hard to
  interpret on their own and are intended for comparing competing approaches
  applied to the same data.

`evaluation()` also stores the complete data coordinates in `compZs`, `compCLPs`
and `complvls`, with the predicted categorical data sets in `GPApred` and
`compPred`. We can use these to draw the two sets of category level points on
top of each other. The orientation of a biplot is arbitrary, so we first rotate
the GPAbin coordinates onto the complete data solution with a small
orthogonal Procrustes helper.

The following figure can be constructed from the available output and is not currently available in the package:

```{r overlay, echo=FALSE}
align_to <- function(testee, target) {
  testee <- scale(testee, scale = FALSE)           
  target <- scale(target, scale = FALSE)
  s   <- svd(crossprod(target, testee))
  rho <- sum(s$d) / sum(testee^2)                  
  rho * testee %*% (s$v %*% t(s$u))                
}

target <- rbind(missbp$compZs[, 1:2],   missbp$compCLPs[, 1:2])
testee <- rbind(missbp$Z.GPAbin[, 1:2], missbp$CLP.GPAbin[, 1:2])
aligned <- align_to(testee, target)
target  <- scale(target, scale = FALSE)

clp_rows <- missbp$n + seq_len(nrow(missbp$CLP.GPAbin))
overlay <- data.frame(
  level = missbp$complvls,
  cx = target[clp_rows, 1],  cy = target[clp_rows, 2],   # complete data
  gx = aligned[clp_rows, 1], gy = aligned[clp_rows, 2]   # GPAbin
)

ggplot(overlay) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = cx, y = cy, xend = gx, yend = gy),
               colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(aes(cx, cy, shape = "Complete data"),
             colour = "#61223b", size = 2.5) +
  geom_point(aes(gx, gy, shape = "GPAbin"),
             colour = "#b79962", size = 3) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(aes(cx, cy, label = level), size = 3) +
  scale_shape_manual(name = NULL,
                     values = c("Complete data" = 16, "GPAbin" = 15)) +
  coord_fixed() +
  theme_void() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Each grey segment links a category level's position in the complete data
biplot to its position in the GPAbin biplot. Most segments are short: even with
about a quarter of the attitude responses missing, the unified display stays
close to the picture we would have obtained with no missing data. The largest
displacements occur for the rarely chosen extreme categories (such as `A:5` and
`C:5`), which are the hardest to place when many of their responses are
missing.

## Already have your imputations?

`impute()` is a convenience. If you prefer to create the imputations yourself,
for example with `mice`, pass the list of completed data sets straight to
`missmi()`. A list is recognised as "already imputed", so `impute()` is
skipped.

```{r own-imputations}
imp <- mice::mice(missdat, m = 5, method = "polyreg", maxit = 5,
                  printFlag = FALSE, seed = 1)
implist_own <- mice::complete(imp, "all")   # list of 5 completed data frames

own <- missmi(implist_own) |> DRT() |> GPAbin()
own
```

The package also includes ready-made simulated examples, `missdat` (a data
frame with about 35% missing values), `implist` (five imputations of it) and
`compdat` (the complete data), which are handy for trying out the functions
quickly:

```{r quick, eval = FALSE}
data(implist)
missmi(implist) |> DRT() |> GPAbin() |> plot() |> evaluation(compdat = compdat)
```


## Good to know

* The current version supports categorical variables and MCA only.
* The biplot is displayed in two dimensions; the GPA alignment itself uses all
  available dimensions.
* The lower-level building blocks are exported: `GPA()` (generalised
  Procrustes analysis of any list of configurations), `OPA()` (orthogonal
  Procrustes analysis) and `CLPpred()` (predicting categories from a biplot).
  See their help pages for details.
* The `GPAbin` approach is not limited to imputations: it can combine
  variations of a visualisation of the same data, such as bootstrap resamples or data collected over time.
